title: Alternative Risk Transfer: Weather Derivatives, Energy Pricing, Real Options, and Catastrophe Bonds
prerequisites: Option payoff profiles and basic risk management
learningOutcomes: Explain why weather, electricity, and catastrophe risks represent incomplete markets where Black-Scholes replication breaks down ([fact-01]).
Calculate cumulative Heating Degree Days (HDD) and Cooling Degree Days (CDD) and price weather options via historical burn analysis ([fact-02], [fact-03], [fact-07]).
Analyze mean-reverting energy spot prices, electricity load profiles, and natural gas storage as real American swing options ([fact-04], [fact-05], [fact-06], [fact-10]).
Evaluate Catastrophe (CAT) bond structures, trigger types, and portfolio diversification benefits ([fact-08], [fact-09], [fact-11]).

sections.title: Energy Derivatives, Mean-Reversion, and Real Options

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: They represent incomplete markets because weather events and bulk electricity cannot be bought and stored in warehouses; BSM replication breaks down, requiring historical burn analysis [fact-01].

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Electricity must be generated and consumed instantaneously in real time, causing grid bottlenecks that generate violent short-term price spikes and negative prices rather than smooth geometric random walks [fact-05].

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: CAT bonds specifically transfer severe natural disaster risks (hurricanes, earthquakes) where principal is forgiven to pay insurer claims upon a predefined catastrophe rather than corporate insolvency [fact-08].

activeRecallQuiz.scenario: A utility company buys a cumulative CDD call option for Chicago covering July with strike K = 300 CDD degree-days and tick size $10,000 per degree day. Over 30 years of historical data, the average payout was 25 degree-days. A 10% risk premium is added.
activeRecallQuiz.question: 1) What is the expected payout and fair market option premium? 2) Why must weather derivatives rely on historical burn analysis instead of BSM storage arbitrage?
activeRecallQuiz.correctAnswer: Correctly identifying the downside risk and margin constraints.
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: Detailed pedagogical explanation grounded in source principles.

coreTakeaways: Incomplete markets like weather and electricity cannot be replicated via BSM storage arbitrage, requiring historical burn analysis and actuarial pricing ([fact-01], [fact-03]).
Energy spot prices exhibit mean reversion toward long-run production costs, while natural gas storage facilities operate as real American swing options ([fact-06], [fact-10]).

Catastrophe bonds transfer natural disaster risk to capital markets via SPVs and various triggers, expanding the efficient frontier with uncorrelated high-yield returns ([fact-08], [fact-09], [fact-11]).
